# Chapter 1: The Briefing

[[Erika]]

The briefing room was cold in the way that meant someone had left the ventilation running overnight.

Forty seats, thirty-nine empty. The display wall at the front showed a single coordinate string, blinking at one-second intervals. Someone had typed it in and walked away.

Erika stood at the terminal and read the string twice. She did not recognize the coordinates, but her hands were already pulling up the tactical overlay before she had finished reading them.

"...promise me."

She stopped. The voice was not in the room. It was the same half-heard fragment she had been carrying for three days, arriving without warning and departing without echo. She waited for it to resolve into something she could hold onto. It did not.

"Doctor."

She turned. Katyusha was in the doorway, her orange braid still damp from the rain outside. She held two mugs and had the expression of someone who had already decided what the morning was going to be.

[[Katyusha]]

"Tea. You haven't slept."

[[Erika]]

"I have slept."

[[Katyusha]]

"You have sat in a chair with your eyes closed. That is not the same thing."

She set the mugs down on the terminal desk and looked at the coordinate string on the display wall. Her eyes moved across it once, the way someone reads a sentence they already know by heart.

[[Katyusha]]

"Those are the northern coordinates."

[[Erika]]

"You know them?"

[[Katyusha]]

"I know what they mean."

---

The corridor to the armory was empty at this hour. Their footsteps echoed off the concrete in a rhythm that matched without either of them adjusting for it.

Nadeshiko was already there, standing at the weapons rack with her back to the door. She did not turn when they entered. She was holding a sidearm in each hand, weighing them with the absent precision of someone who had done this ten thousand times before and no longer needed to look.

"Nadeshiko," Erika said. "We have a deployment."

Nadeshiko set both sidearms down on the rack, carefully, the way someone sets down an argument they have decided to finish later.

She turned. Her eyes moved from Erika to Katyusha and back.

"Nadeshiko, from the weapons rack: 'Which one this time?'" Erika said, and the words came out wrong, the attribution tangled with the dialogue in a way that made her pause.

Nadeshiko looked at her for a moment that was longer than a moment.

"It does not matter which one," she said. "They all work the same way."

[[Maria]]

Maria arrived from the east corridor with a data tablet under one arm and the expression of someone who had been reading for too long without looking up. Her dark hair was pulled back in a style that suggested she had better things to worry about than hair.

"The signal source is confirmed," she said, before anyone asked. "Sector seven, grid reference fourteen. The same one Erika flagged three days ago."

[[Erika]]

"Three days ago I was not sure."

[[Maria]]

"You are sure now."

It was not a question. Erika did not answer it.

---

The transport bay was cold and smelled of ozone and burnt hydraulic fluid. Seven crates were lined up along the south wall, each one sealed with the blue stripe that meant active deployment.

[[Drona]]

Drona was already loading the last crate onto the transport bed when they arrived. She did not look up. Her movements were exact and unhurried, the movements of someone who had decided that speed was a problem someone else could have.

"Drona," Erika said. "We are moving in twenty minutes."

Drona finished sealing the crate before she answered.

"I know," she said. "I am moving in fifteen."

Katyusha stood at the transport bay door, arms crossed, watching the loading with the patience of someone who had already counted every crate and confirmed every seal.

[[Katyusha]]

"Oracle is online."

[[Erika]]

"When is Oracle not online?"

[[Katyusha]]

"When the network drops. Which happened at oh-three-hundred this morning. For eleven minutes."

Erika looked at the coordinate string on her data tablet. The same string from the briefing room. The same string that had been blinking on the display wall when she arrived.

"Eleven minutes is enough," she said.

Katyusha said nothing. That was its own kind of answer.

The transport engine coughed once, caught, and settled into a steady hum. Outside, the rain had stopped. The sky was the flat grey of something that had not yet decided whether to clear or get worse.

Erika climbed into the transport and took the seat facing the rear. Her hands were steady now. She did not trust that.
